passage:
The composer Morton Feldman occupies an unusual position in twentieth-century music history: celebrated by a small but devoted critical following, yet persistently relegated to the margins of concert programming and popular musicological accounts. Standard histories of postwar American music tend to cast the 1950s as a contest between serialist rigor—exemplified by Milton Babbitt's densely calculated pitch rows—and the theatrical indeterminacy of John Cage, whose chance procedures and conceptual provocations dominated the avant-garde conversation. Feldman, despite his long personal friendship with Cage, fits neither category comfortably, and this categorical awkwardness has too often been mistaken for aesthetic lesser importance.

The truth is that Feldman's music, particularly the series of works he titled Projections and Intersections from the early 1950s, represents a third path that illuminates the limits of both prevailing models. The serialists prized precision: every note generated from a master numerical system, every parameter controlled. Cage prized release: the composer's ego dissolved into accident and environmental noise. Feldman wanted neither control nor its deliberate abdication. His scores notated duration and dynamics with unusual care while leaving specific pitches to the performer's discretion—a balance that contemporaries found difficult to classify and critics have since struggled to name. The term most often applied, "indeterminate," is technically accurate but misleading, implying a kinship with Cage that flattens the critical difference: where Cage welcomed noise and disruption as music's raw material, Feldman regarded sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention. His characteristic dynamic was pianissimo; his characteristic gesture, a soft chord appearing briefly and then retreating into silence.

This attention to the quality of individual sounds—what Feldman called "sounds as sounds" rather than sounds as symbols or structural arguments—aligns him more productively with the visual artists of his New York circle than with his fellow composers. He counted the painters Philip Guston and Mark Rothko among his closest interlocutors, and the influence ran both ways. Rothko's late canvases, with their hovering rectangular forms that seem to materialize and then dissolve at the canvas's edges, pursue a visual analogue to what Feldman was achieving acoustically: presence without insistence, form without argument. To call Feldman's music abstract expressionist in a strictly programmatic sense would be imprecise; but to ignore how deeply his aesthetic was shaped by painters who believed that a work of art could create an immediate, almost physical encounter with feeling, without narrative or explanation, is to miss the animating impulse of everything he wrote.

Feldman's relative obscurity, then, reflects not a poverty of achievement but the poverty of the categories through which postwar music has been filtered. A criticism adequate to his work would need to set aside the serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis entirely and attend instead to the phenomenology of listening—to what it feels like when a sound appears, persists briefly, and vanishes—and to the ethics of restraint that Feldman practiced with a consistency no other composer of his generation matched.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Morton Feldman's friendship with John Cage led him to develop a form of musical indeterminacy that surpassed Cage's own experiments.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Postwar American music is best understood as a contest between serialist precision and Cagean indeterminacy, within which Feldman found a compromise position.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Feldman's marginalization in music history reflects the inadequacy of standard critical categories rather than any deficiency in his work, and a better criticism would attend to the phenomenology of his sound.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The visual artists of the New York school exerted a decisive and underappreciated influence on all major postwar American composers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Feldman's scores are technically indeterminate because they leave specific pitches to the performer's discretion, placing him firmly within the Cagean tradition.

explanations.correct: The passage argues throughout that Feldman's obscurity stems from categorical inadequacy (serialist vs. indeterminate axis) rather than aesthetic weakness, and closes by calling for a criticism grounded in phenomenology and restraint. C captures both strands of this integrated thesis.
explanations.A: The passage explicitly distinguishes Feldman from Cage; there is no claim that Feldman surpassed Cage. This answer misrepresents the relationship.
explanations.B: The passage directly contradicts this framing: Feldman 'fits neither category comfortably,' and the passage's thesis rejects the serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis as an adequate lens.
explanations.C: Correct. This integrates the diagnosis (marginalization due to bad categories) with the prescription (phenomenological criticism), matching the full arc of the passage.
explanations.D: Too broad — the passage discusses Feldman's relationship with painters, not all major postwar composers. This answer overgeneralizes from a specific claim.
explanations.E: The passage calls 'indeterminate' technically accurate but misleading and explicitly argues against grouping Feldman with Cage. This answer restates a claim the author disputes.

questions.questionStem: The author's attitude toward standard histories of postwar American music can best be described as

choices.label: A
choices.text: qualified admiration for their rigorous documentation of serialism and indeterminacy

choices.label: B
choices.text: critical skepticism about the adequacy of the frameworks they impose

choices.label: C
choices.text: enthusiastic endorsement of their account of the Feldman–Cage relationship

choices.label: D
choices.text: mild curiosity about how they came to overlook Feldman's connections to visual art

choices.label: E
choices.text: outright rejection of every claim they make about postwar American composers

explanations.correct: The author repeatedly challenges the standard historical framework: it 'too often' mistakes categorical awkwardness for lesser importance, the 'indeterminate' label is misleading, and the 'serialist-versus-indeterminacy axis' must be 'set aside entirely.' This constitutes sustained critical skepticism about the frameworks — not outright rejection of all content, but skepticism about the organizing categories.
explanations.A: The passage offers no admiration for these histories; it argues they have distorted the understanding of Feldman. 'Admiration' is the wrong valence.
explanations.B: Correct. The author's repeated challenge to the standard two-camp framework — calling it inadequate and misleading — is best characterized as critical skepticism.
explanations.C: The author does not endorse the standard account of Feldman and Cage; on the contrary, the passage argues the kinship implied by that account is misleading.
explanations.D: 'Mild curiosity' is far too weak; the author makes a sustained argument, not a passing inquiry. This understates the author's critical engagement.
explanations.E: The author accepts that the serialist–Cage contrast is a real historical phenomenon; the critique is of the framework's inadequacy, not the factual claims within it. 'Outright rejection' overstates the author's position.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A composer is introduced; his works are chronologically surveyed; a comparison with visual artists is proposed; his place in music history is evaluated.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A prevailing critical framework is described; a composer who escapes it is introduced and examined on his own terms; cross-disciplinary affinities are identified; a call for better critical tools is issued.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Two competing aesthetic movements are described; a composer who synthesizes them is celebrated; his debt to painting is explained; a historical revisionism is proposed.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A composer's obscurity is lamented; the musicians who influenced him are identified; the visual artists he influenced are discussed; a new biography is recommended.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A contrast between Feldman and Cage is developed across three paragraphs and then resolved by showing that both belong to the same tradition.

explanations.correct: Paragraph 1 describes the prevailing serialist-vs.-Cage framework. Paragraph 2 introduces Feldman as escaping that framework and examines his scores. Paragraph 3 identifies his affinities with New York painters. Paragraph 4 calls for a phenomenological critical approach. B tracks these four moves accurately.
explanations.A: The passage does not offer a chronological survey of Feldman's works; only the early Projections and Intersections are named. The sequence of moves described in A does not match.
explanations.B: Correct. This accurately captures the four-paragraph arc: framework, third-path composer, cross-disciplinary affinities, call for new criticism.
explanations.C: The passage argues Feldman does not synthesize the two movements but transcends their axis altogether. 'Synthesizes' misrepresents the author's claim.
explanations.D: The passage does not identify musicians who influenced Feldman, nor does it recommend a biography. This answer introduces moves the passage never makes.
explanations.E: The passage argues the opposite: Feldman and Cage belong to different traditions despite their personal friendship. The contrast is sustained, not resolved into unity.

questions.questionStem: According to the passage, Feldman's scores for the Projections and Intersections series differed from serialist scores in that Feldman's scores

choices.label: A
choices.text: specified dynamics and duration precisely but left specific pitches to the performer

choices.label: B
choices.text: dissolved compositional ego entirely through the use of chance procedures

choices.label: C
choices.text: generated every parameter, including pitch, from a master numerical system

choices.label: D
choices.text: welcomed environmental noise as the primary raw material for composition

choices.label: E
choices.text: left both pitch and duration to the performer's discretion in order to achieve indeterminacy

explanations.correct: The passage states explicitly that Feldman's scores 'notated duration and dynamics with unusual care while leaving specific pitches to the performer's discretion.' A paraphrases this precisely.
explanations.A: Correct. This is a direct paraphrase of the passage's description of Feldman's scoring practice.
explanations.B: This describes Cage's approach, not Feldman's. The passage distinguishes Feldman from Cage on exactly this point.
explanations.C: This describes the serialist method (Babbitt's 'densely calculated pitch rows'), which the passage explicitly contrasts with Feldman's practice.
explanations.D: Welcoming environmental noise is attributed to Cage, not Feldman. The passage says Feldman 'regarded sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention' — the opposite of welcoming noise.
explanations.E: The passage specifies that duration was notated with care; only pitch was left to the performer. Leaving both indeterminate contradicts the passage's description.

questions.questionStem: The passage most strongly suggests that which one of the following is true of Mark Rothko's late paintings?

choices.label: A
choices.text: They were directly inspired by Feldman's musical scores for the Projections series.

choices.label: B
choices.text: They achieve their effect through the suggestion of form that emerges and recedes rather than through fixed, assertive structure.

choices.label: C
choices.text: They exemplify the serialist principle that every visual parameter should be systematically controlled.

choices.label: D
choices.text: They were widely celebrated in postwar American music criticism as a model for composers.

choices.label: E
choices.text: They prioritize narrative and explanation over immediate sensory encounter.

explanations.correct: The passage describes Rothko's late canvases as having 'hovering rectangular forms that seem to materialize and then dissolve at the canvas's edges,' pursuing 'presence without insistence, form without argument.' B captures this inference — form that emerges and recedes rather than asserting itself — without overstating.
explanations.A: The passage says the influence between Feldman and the painters 'ran both ways,' but it does not assert that Rothko's paintings were directly inspired by the Projections scores specifically. This overreaches the passage's claim.
explanations.B: Correct. 'Materialize and then dissolve,' 'presence without insistence, form without argument' — all support the inference that Rothko's forms suggest rather than assert, emerge and recede.
explanations.C: Serialism is associated with Babbitt and the composers, not with Rothko. Applying a serialist description to Rothko contradicts the passage's framing of the two as analogous, not identical.
explanations.D: The passage says Rothko was among Feldman's interlocutors; it makes no claim about music criticism celebrating Rothko as a model for composers.
explanations.E: The passage explicitly states Rothko and Feldman shared a belief that art could create 'an immediate, almost physical encounter with feeling, without narrative or explanation.' E directly contradicts this.

questions.questionStem: The author's discussion of Cage's use of chance procedures and environmental noise (second paragraph) serves primarily to

choices.label: A
choices.text: celebrate Cage's contribution to the avant-garde as a necessary precondition for Feldman's own innovations

choices.label: B
choices.text: establish a contrast that clarifies what was distinctive and irreducible about Feldman's relationship to sound

choices.label: C
choices.text: demonstrate that Cage's approach was more radical than serialism and therefore more historically significant

choices.label: D
choices.text: support the claim that Feldman belongs squarely within the indeterminate tradition that Cage established

choices.label: E
choices.text: introduce a counterexample that the author subsequently concedes undermines the case for Feldman's originality

explanations.correct: The passage invokes Cage's 'welcome of noise and disruption' precisely to sharpen the contrast with Feldman's 'hushed, almost reverential attention' to sound. The function is contrastive: the Cage description clarifies what Feldman was not doing and why the 'indeterminate' label misleads.
explanations.A: The passage does not frame Cage's work as a precondition for Feldman's; on the contrary, it argues Feldman's path was independent of and distinct from Cage's, despite their friendship.
explanations.B: Correct. The discussion of Cage immediately precedes and motivates the sentence about Feldman regarding 'sound itself with a hushed, almost reverential attention' — a contrastive function.
explanations.C: The passage makes no comparative judgment about historical significance between Cage and the serialists. This answer introduces a claim the passage does not make.
explanations.D: The passage argues the opposite: the discussion of Cage is designed to show that calling Feldman 'indeterminate' implies a misleading kinship with Cage.
explanations.E: The author never concedes that Cage's work undermines Feldman's originality; the entire passage argues for Feldman's distinctiveness. This inverts the author's argument.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following situations most closely conforms to the principle the author invokes in arguing that the label 'indeterminate' is misleading when applied to Feldman's music?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A novelist is categorized as a realist because her books describe everyday domestic life, even though her prose style is highly experimental and her thematic concerns are closer to those of the symbolists.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A filmmaker is praised as an auteur because she writes, directs, and edits her own films, a practice she shares with several other celebrated directors.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A sculptor is grouped with minimalists because he uses industrial materials, despite the fact that minimalism itself is a diverse movement with no single defining criterion.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A jazz pianist is called a traditionalist because he plays standard repertoire, and this label accurately captures his approach to improvisation, harmony, and rhythm.

choices.label: E
choices.text: A poet is described as a romanticist because she uses rhyme and meter, features she shares with romantic poets, even though her subject matter is exclusively political satire.

explanations.correct: The passage's principle is: a technically accurate label ('indeterminate') is applied to Feldman because of a surface feature he shares with Cage (performer discretion over pitch), but that label obscures a critical difference in underlying aesthetic orientation (reverence vs. welcome of noise). A mirrors this exactly: 'realist' is applied because of a surface feature (domestic subject matter), but the label obscures a critical difference in aesthetic orientation (symbolist, experimental style).
explanations.A: Correct. The shared surface feature (domestic settings / pitch discretion) justifies the label technically, but the deeper aesthetic orientation diverges sharply — exactly the structure the passage describes.
explanations.B: This describes a case where a label is applied because of shared practice, and the label seems accurate; there is no misleading suppression of a critical difference. The auteur label is not shown to flatten any important distinction.
explanations.C: This describes label imprecision due to the category's own internal diversity, not because the label suppresses a critical difference between the labeled artist and the category's paradigm case. The mechanism differs.
explanations.D: Here the label accurately captures the artist's approach across multiple dimensions. This is the opposite of the passage's principle, which concerns technically-accurate-but-misleading labels.
explanations.E: Close, but in E the divergence (political satire) is primarily one of subject matter rather than underlying aesthetic orientation and the way the work engages its medium — the passage's principle concerns orientation toward the artistic medium itself (sound as reverence vs. sound as accident), not merely thematic content.
